paper_metadata.title: Quantum machine learning for quantum anomaly detection

summary: This paper proposes two gate-based quantum anomaly-detection algorithms: quantum kernel PCA and quantum one-class SVM, each for pure and mixed quantum states. The main quantitative claim is asymptotic resource scaling of O(poly(M log d)) for overlap-based protocols, with a more advanced pure-state one-class SVM protocol using HHL to obtain O(log M) runtime under strong assumptions; no experimental hardware results are reported.

experiments.description: Quantum kernel PCA for anomaly detection on pure quantum states, including a logarithmic-in-dimension protocol and an alternative logarithmic-in-dimension-and-training-size protocol.

algorithm.variant: quantum kernel PCA for anomaly detection (pure states)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Quantum states |ψ_i⟩ are treated as data vectors; centroid and centered states are formed in the Hilbert space. No explicit qubit-to-variable binary encoding is used.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Detect anomalies by computing proximity measure f(ψ0)=⟨z0|(1-C)|z0⟩, where C is the centered covariance operator built from training states.

problem_instance.description: Anomaly detection among a training set of M unknown pure quantum states and a test pure state |ψ0⟩; intended for detecting outliers in manufactured quantum circuits or other quantum data.

dataset_specification.description: Unknown pure quantum states generated by quantum devices; no public benchmark specified.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Construct centroid state |ψc⟩, centered states |zi⟩, and centered test state |z0⟩ from the training and test quantum states.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Theoretical resource analysis; proximity measure estimated via modified swap tests. No numerical benchmark or empirical dataset split reported.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Compute inner products ⟨ψ_i|ψ_κ⟩ via modified swap tests; compute normalization constants N_c and N_i from overlaps.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Assemble proximity measure f(ψ0) from estimated overlaps and normalization constants.

speedup_claims.factor: logarithmic in d; potentially logarithmic in M for pure states
speedup_claims.baseline_method: state tomography / classical reconstruction of quantum states
speedup_claims.conditions: assuming access to state-preparation unitaries and, for the HHL-based protocol, efficient matrix inversion and low-rank kernel structure
speedup_claims.caveats: No empirical benchmark; resource scaling is asymptotic and depends on being able to prepare centroid/centered states and estimate overlaps with modified swap tests.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(poly(M log d)) for the first protocol; O(log d) resources for measuring the proximity with the second protocol once C is prepared; overall logarithmic in d and potentially in M for pure states.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Not explicitly characterized for the anomaly-detection task; state tomography is cited as requiring exponentially more measurements in d.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: The paper claims logarithmic scaling in d and, for pure states, potentially logarithmic scaling in M, but provides no hardware implementation or empirical crossover study.
limiting_factors: Requires access to controlled unitaries for state preparation
Relies on modified swap tests and repeated measurements
State-preparation and overlap-estimation overheads dominate practical feasibility

notes: No specific hardware platform, qubit count, or circuit depth is given; the paper is a theoretical algorithmic proposal.
num_qubits and circuit_depth are null because the paper discusses resource scaling rather than a concrete implementation.
The paper is a theoretical proposal; no classical-vs-quantum benchmark is reported.

experiments.description: Quantum one-class SVM for anomaly detection on pure quantum states, including a swap-test-based protocol and an HHL-based matrix-inversion protocol.

algorithm.variant: quantum one-class SVM for anomaly detection (pure states), least-squares formulation

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Training states |ψ_i⟩ define a fidelity kernel matrix; the linear system for α is solved quantumly via HHL in the advanced protocol.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Find hyperplane parameters α_i such that f(ψ0)=|Σ_i α_i |⟨ψ_i|ψ0⟩|^2 - 1| is small for normal states and large for anomalies.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Least-squares one-class SVM with threshold acceptance probability PT; bias fixed to r=1 in the main formulation.

problem_instance.description: Anomaly detection among M pure quantum training states and a test pure state |ψ0⟩.

dataset_specification.description: Unknown pure quantum states; no public benchmark specified.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Construct kernel matrix K from pairwise fidelities |⟨ψ_i|ψ_j⟩|^2; solve for α_i; evaluate proximity on test state.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Theoretical resource analysis; no empirical benchmark or hardware run reported.

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical matrix inversion is used in the simpler protocol; HHL is used in the advanced protocol.
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Estimate kernel entries via swap tests; in the simpler protocol, perform classical O(M^3) matrix inversion to obtain α_i.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute f(ψ0)=|Σ_i α_i |⟨ψ_i|ψ0⟩|^2 - 1| using overlap estimates.

classical_baselines.method_name: classical overlap estimation via swap tests

speedup_claims.factor: logarithmic in M and d under HHL-based protocol
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical matrix inversion and pairwise kernel estimation
speedup_claims.conditions: requires access to the control unitary UC, efficient exponentiation of the kernel matrix, low-rank structure, and condition number at most O(log M)
speedup_claims.caveats: The simpler protocol still requires O(M^2 log d) kernel estimation and O(M^3) classical inversion; the logarithmic-in-M claim is conditional on HHL assumptions.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^2 log d) to estimate all kernel entries plus O(M^3) classical inversion in the simpler protocol; O(log M) runtime for HHL-based matrix inversion under stated assumptions, with O(poly(M log d)) total resources for proximity evaluation.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(M^3) for matrix inversion; O(M^2 log d) for kernel estimation via swap tests.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: The HHL-based protocol is claimed to run in O(log M) time under strong assumptions, but the paper does not provide a practical crossover size or implementation.
limiting_factors: Requires efficient matrix inversion via HHL
Assumes low-rank kernel matrix and favorable condition number
Requires controlled access to the training-state preparation unitary
No empirical comparison against classical baselines

notes: No concrete qubit register size or circuit depth is specified; the paper provides asymptotic resource scaling only.
The simpler protocol explicitly uses classical matrix inversion; this is not a separate experiment.
The paper gives asymptotic resource estimates only; no demonstrated advantage on real hardware.

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Assemble the mixed-state proximity measure f(ρ0) from estimated overlaps.
